text: The top comment is right about the percentage, but the number that actually measures spacing isn't percentage at all. It's attempts. A guy shooting 35% on real volume gets guarded past the line, because his defender has to respect it. A guy at 40% who takes two a game does not, because his defender has already done that math. Spacing is entirely about whether the defender leaves, and only volume makes him leave. So for this roster I'd look at 3PA per 36 across the starters rather than their percentages. That'll tell you how much room the drives actually have.

text: I would argue for a First Contract exception. If you draft a player or trade for them while on their rookie deal their contract is discounted against the cap 1% for every year of service. Example: a player signs a max contract with 10 years of service for 35% of the cap. That contract only counts as 25% of the cap. If a team goes into the second apron while they are using the FCE they lose the ability to use that exception for 3 years. You only have one FCE exception to use every year. The idea is you give teams extra flexibility to build around their stars as they age. Everyone wants stars to stay with the team drafted them and I think most people don’t want to watch aging superstars waste their post prime on terrible teams. 10% isn’t going push a team from average to contender but it might give enough flexibility for a team to go from good to contender.
label: analytical

That's an identity rather than a coincidence. TS% is defined as PTS/(2*TSA), so points above average = 2 * TSA * (TS% - lgTS%), which is exactly twice your formula. UW-rTS is points above average per 100 possessions in half units. That isn't a knock on the idea. The Chandler vs Curry comparison is the right motivation and rTS genuinely does need a volume term next to it.
